topicData.topic:
AI is triggering one of the largest infrastructure build-outs in history, with trillions of dollars expected to flow into data centres, GPUs, power and computing capacity. A new class of “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave, Crusoe and Nscale is emerging by building and renting this infrastructure to AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

Direction on post - Write an engaging, human-sounding LinkedIn post around the idea that the AI boom is becoming an infrastructure gold rush. Start with a surprising number, deal or observation rather than explaining AI. Show how companies like OpenAI and Anthropic need enormous amounts of rented compute, creating a new generation of infrastructure businesses—the “picks and shovels” of AI.

Keep the language conversational and curious, not corporate or overly polished. Use short paragraphs and build the story naturally: huge AI demand → massive infrastructure investment → rise of neoclouds → the bigger business question. Avoid generic phrases such as “AI is transforming the world,” excessive statistics, buzzwords, headings, and obvious AI-written formatting.

End with a thoughtful question: as trillions flow into AI infrastructure, will the biggest winners of the AI boom be the companies building the models—or the companies owning the compute, power and infrastructure underneath them?
topicData.angle: Write from the specific details and your honest reaction to this topic.

postText:
$11.9 billion. One contract. Between two companies most people outside tech could not have named three years ago.

@CoreWeave just signed that deal with @OpenAI. And the detail that stopped me isn't the number.

It's that OpenAI — building what many consider the most capable AI systems in the world — doesn't own the computers running them. They rent. At scale. Long-term. Because training these models requires so much compute that even the best-funded AI labs in history can't, or won't, own it all.

So a new category of business is forming to fill that gap.

CoreWeave, Crusoe, Nscale. Companies building data centres, acquiring land near power grids, buying GPUs in bulk, and renting the whole stack back to the AI labs. They're not building the models. They're building the ground the models stand on.

Classic picks and shovels logic. The gold rush metaphor gets overused but it fits here. In the 1840s the consistent money wasn't in the gold. It was in the tools, the transport, the infrastructure that made mining possible at all.

The difference now is the scale. Trillions of dollars are expected to flow into this infrastructure layer over the next decade. Not millions. Not billions as a rounding error. Trillions into power, compute, cooling and the physical real estate to hold it all.

What I find genuinely interesting — and I haven't fully resolved this — is what it means for the AI companies at the top of the stack. Renting compute at this scale creates enormous dependency on a supplier class that didn't really exist five years ago. The neoclouds have long-term contracts and locked-in revenue. The AI labs have the brand and the models but not always the infrastructure underneath them.

That's an unusual power dynamic to build an industry on.

So the honest question: as the money flows into infrastructure at this scale, will the biggest winners of the AI boom be the companies building the models — or the ones who own the compute, the power and the pipes underneath them?

#EnterpriseAI #TechLeadership #DigitalTransformation
